1:
Almost nothing is known of the man, and the voices say as much. Keil and Delitzsch treats the name itself, formed from a root meaning to embrace, so that it may mean either one who embraces or one who is embraced; an older interpreter took the first sense warmly, that the prophet takes his people to his arms as one quiets a weeping child. Clarke calls what the ancients report of him fabulous, and places him before the captivity, since he speaks of the Chaldeans and never of the Assyrians.

Why the title prophet is added divides the voices slightly. Gill reports a Jewish commentator's question, why Habakkuk alone among the lesser prophets should be so styled, apart from Haggai and Zechariah, and the answer that it gives weight to a prophecy some might doubt, since none of the usual formulas occur here. Ellicott notices the same restriction to those three and adds what the word means elsewhere, designating members of the prophetical colleges founded by Samuel and kept up until the days of Elisha; whether it carries that force here, or merely marks a chosen minister, he leaves undecided. Henry thinks the title enough by itself, so that we need not ask about tribe or birthplace, and takes the word burden to imply that the prophet was as sure of what he had to say as if he had seen it accomplished. Wesley reads the burden as something the prophet himself groaned under.

Whose burden it is Calvin contests. The greater part of interpreters refer it to the Chaldeans and the monarchy of Babylon; he cannot approve that, since the prophet addresses the Jews and calls his prophecy a burden without qualification, and the view sits ill with a man who goes on to dread the devastation of his own land. The burden is that God, after long forbearance, would at last punish the sins of the Jews; and Gill takes it the same way, a heavy prophecy carried to that people, declaring the calamities the Chaldeans would bring.

The complaint that follows is read as present rather than anticipated. Calvin reports again that interpreters take the prophet to speak of future things with the coming calamity in view, and calls that too strained: he is expostulating with God for so patiently indulging a people already hardened. Calvin infers that the prophet had long been exercising his office as a teacher, since it would have been improper to open his work with such an expostulation; having found the people perverse, he withdrew from men and addressed God privately, and what we have is that secret colloquy. It is not unfeeling, he adds, that a prophet should wish to hasten vengeance against his own kindred, since he must be concerned not only for the people's safety but for the glory of God. Keil and Delitzsch reaches the same conclusion by exclusion: the lament is uttered for the believers who suffered under the wicked, and not, as some rabbinic and modern interpreters suppose, over the violence the Chaldeans did in the land, but over the ungodly of the prophet's own nation.

Gill reads the how long as an inference that his prayers were unheard. Clarke says he had declaimed against these vices in vain, the people continuing in them and God in his longsuffering,. Ellicott renders the second half so that he cries to God the single word violence, which occurs elsewhere as an appeal for help in the way we cry murder or fire. Henry supplies the state of things behind the cry, that no man could call what he had his own, since whoever had power took what he pleased and the land was full of violence as the old world had been; and the prophet was not himself wronged, but grieved to see others wronged and mingled his tears with theirs.
3:
What the prophet is made to look at is defined by the words. Clarke glosses the second noun as labour and distress and misery, the common fruits of sin. Ellicott renders the whole more exactly, why dost thou show me distress and look upon grievance, oppression and violence are before me, and contention exalts itself;, defining grievance as trouble wilfully caused. He points forward to the later verse about purer eyes than to behold evil as illustrating the question about God looking on. Gill makes it a matter of what filled the prophet's view: he could not turn his eyes anywhere without such men presenting themselves, and their actions were done openly and without shame.

Calvin uses the verse to settle whose wickedness is in view. Those who apply it to the Chaldeans do so strainedly, he says, having failed to observe that the prophet is not teaching the Jews here but preparing them for a coming judgment, which they could not but see was just once the godly had cried out against them. From this he draws a rule: all who really serve God ought, by the prophet's example, to burn with holy indignation when they see wickedness reigning unrestrained, and especially in the Church of God, since nothing ought to grieve us more than to see men raging with profane contempt and all order trodden under foot. To the objection that the prophet exceeded moderation he gives a direct answer. Though he pours forth his feelings freely, nothing wrong is imputed to him; for why do we pray at all, except that each may unburden his cares and griefs by pouring them into the bosom of God? Since God allows such familiarity, no fault attaches to prayers of this kind, provided the bridle of obedience keeps us within bounds.

The slackened law is explained by its effects. Gill takes it that the law is not executed against offenders, the magistrates being dilatory and slow to act for honest men who are oppressed; and he prefers a second rendering, that the law is intermitted, like a man whose pulse beats so low it is scarcely felt, which shows the body politic out of health when the law, its soul, is not allowed to do its office. Ellicott says the same in his own terms, that the law which ought to be a bond of security is paralysed and unable to work, and that judgment, meaning the redress of evils, never goes forth because the wicked have hemmed the righteous in, so that no sentence issues except such as favours them. Wesley states the cause and extends the reference: this follows because the wicked go on with impunity, the law meant is the whole law, moral and ceremonial and judicial, and the compassing about is a besieging with design to oppress. Clarke adds the sequel: right judgment is never pronounced and the righteous complain in vain, but when judgment does not proceed from the seat of judgment on earth it will infallibly go forth from the throne of judgment in heaven.

Calvin returns to the prophet's own motive, and turns it on the reader. He was not moved by carnal passion, as happens with us when we are injured, for then a man is incensed at once while letting God's law be made a sport; we are tender only where we ourselves are touched, and easily forgive an injury done to God. The prophet's indignation was not private but rose from the profanation of God's worship. Let us learn to rouse ourselves, Calvin says, since we are frigid when the ungodly openly mock God; and he cites the apostolic word be ye angry and sin not, which shows there is just occasion for anger, so that a man should regard his own sins until he becomes his own enemy, and be indignant whenever he sees God offended.
5:
Henry hears the answer to the complaint, and its temper: though God bore long he will not bear always, and no resentments are so keen as those of abused patience. He lists what punishment is threatened. It is public, aggravating the desolation by making the sufferers a spectacle to the world. It is amazing, so far out of the common road of providence that it will not be credited even by those who had the prediction beforehand, since it seems incredible that God should deal so severely with a people he had taken into covenant. It is speedy, worked in their own days, and a work of God's own working, so that all who see it must say this is the Lord's doing; and it is a type of a later ruin, the words being applied in the Acts to the despisers of the gospel.

Whom the looking is addressed to is disputed. Gill insists the words are spoken to the Jews and not to the heathen, calling them to observe how the king of Babylon had overturned the Assyrian empire and was subduing one people after another, so their own turn would come quickly. Wesley reads the clause as pointing to precedent, what judgments have been executed on the heathen for like sins. Ellicott takes the words as emphatic in another way, implying that God will no longer manifest himself among his own people but among the Gentiles; they are to wonder not at the choice of agent but at the consequences, the sack of the Temple and the carrying away of ten thousand captives. Calvin turns the phrase into a rebuke. God might have bidden them look to himself, but having spent his labour in vain he sets the Chaldeans over them as teachers, so that they learn from the Gentiles what they refused to learn from his own mouth; and he notes how the alarm is raised by repetition, they being twice bidden to see and twice to wonder.

A textual question runs under the verse, which Gill notices in passing, the old versions rendering it in a way that agrees better with the apostle's quotation. Clarke reports that some critics would read a word meaning transgressors in place of the word meaning nations, that the versions read so, and that the apostle quotes it in that form; but no such reading, he adds, is found in any manuscript yet collated. Ellicott judges that the Greek translators probably misread the word, which is where the despisers of the citation come from, and holds that the citation gives it no authority; nor is it certain, he adds, that the apostle did not quote the Hebrew form, which would suit his circumstances better. Calvin says only that the Greek translators no doubt read the other word.

On the instrument the voices divide over its history. Gill describes a people lately mean and low, famous only for soothsaying and astrology, now grown warlike and rising toward universal monarchy. Ellicott allows that the phrase implies the Chaldeans were not yet in the land, but denies any allusion to a recent rise of the nation, and reports an ethnological theory, now generally abandoned, which made these Chaldeans a distinct race of northern hordes lately arrived and raised on a sudden from the estate of colonists. Clarke and Wesley agree on the epithets, cruel and without mercy, prompt and speedy; Keil and Delitzsch renders the pair fierce and vehement, a nation marching the breadths of the earth to possess dwelling-places not its own. Calvin explains why the naming was needed: it was not enough to speak generally of a work of God without saying that destruction by the Chaldeans was at hand, the prophets differing from Moses in showing as with a finger what he threatened generally. That was necessary, he says, because the people despised denunciations however plainly set before their eyes.
7:
Gill accounts for the terror by what produced it: the fierceness of their countenances, the number of their troops, the splendour of their armour, the victories already won and the cruelty already exercised, the fame of which went before them. Calvin warns that in calling them terrible the prophet is not praising their virtues but showing that they were fitted to do God's service in executing his vengeance, since he so regulated his judgment as to use their cruelty for a good purpose. That leads him further. The worst of men are in God's hand, as Satan is who is their head, and yet God is not implicated in their wickedness, though some maintain that if he governs by providence he becomes the author of sin; Scripture teaches otherwise, that the wicked are led by his hidden power, that the fault remains theirs when they act cruelly, and that God is just whatever instruments he uses.

The clause about judgment proceeding of themselves is read three ways that agree in substance. Wesley says the law they observe is their own will and their authority is all from themselves, without respect to any other rule. Ellicott makes their judgment a claim to adjudge the affairs of mankind, proceeding from themselves as irresponsible and recognising no supreme being as the source of justice, their dignity likewise self-sustained and unsanctioned. Calvin illustrates by contrast: a man who obeys laws will allow judges in a dispute, but one who will have everything done according to his own purpose repudiates all judges, and so these would be their own judges. Clarke alone reads it historically, that by revolting from the Assyrians they had made themselves a great nation, so that their judgment and their excellence were the fruit of their own valour; and he grants that other meanings are given to the passage.

On the animals the voices become naturalists. Gill reports from ancient writers that nothing is swifter than the panther and that it overtakes most creatures by its running, and passes on an old account of the animal's parentage which he corrects in one particular. Clarke says the leopard of all quadrupeds is allowed the swiftest, calls the Chaldean cavalry proverbial for swiftness, and cites an ancient poet on the horses bred beside the great river, warhorses by nature, so intrepid that neither the sight nor the roaring of a lion appals them. Calvin explains why the point had to be pressed: the Jews might have eluded the threatening by thinking the Chaldeans far off and the danger not near, and so the prophet says their horses are swifter than leopards.

The evening wolves are explained by hunger. Calvin says the wolf is a rapacious animal, and that when he has ranged all day in vain his hunger kindles rage toward evening, so that there is nothing more dreadful than a hungry wolf. Wesley says they fasted through the day and came out at evening fierce and ravenous. Ellicott corrects the rendering, since the verb means sharper rather than more fierce, and takes the ideas to be activity and ferocity prompted by hunger, the evening wolf leaving his lair being elsewhere a standing figure of greediness. Clarke turns to the animal's sight, and cites an ancient writer that a wolf can see by night even when there is no moonlight; he reports too that some think a different beast is meant, swift and cruel and untameable. Ellicott adds a note on a parallel in another prophet, where chariots are as a whirlwind and horses swifter than eagles: it is very like this verse, but neither need be made the original or the echo of the other, since both rest on an older song. Calvin corrects one more word, that the verb rendered spreading themselves does not mean various, as some give it, but to range at large or spread far and wide.
9:
Gill takes the whole army to be meant, every one coming with a single view, not to do themselves justice or avenge an affront but purely for spoil; Wesley says the same, that they came to enrich themselves by making a prey of all. Calvin draws an inference: to say they come for the prey is to say they will have no labour and be victorious before there is any contest, since the Jews would be frightened and submit at once. He turns that into a general observation, that God so debilitates the hearts of those who resist his word that men grown strong against him cannot stand before their fellow-mortals; and the point here was to keep the Jews from hoping anything from the chance of war.

The clause about their faces is the most disputed in the chapter. Wesley keeps the received rendering and says their very countenances shall be as blasting as the east wind. Clarke keeps it too and illustrates it from a traveller's report of the electric winds of that country, one of which passed over a man coming out of a river and in a moment carried off every particle of water from him; so, Clarke says, the Chaldeans will leave no substance behind. Calvin works from the root, which he says means what is opposite, and notes that the east wind was very injurious to that land and dried up its vegetation. Ellicott states the difficulty plainly. If the word could mean east wind, the invading host would be a blast from the east leaving the land scorched, and the captives would answer to the cloud of dust that accompanies such a blast, which gives a good sense; but all analogy, he says, requires the word to mean either eastwards or forwards, while the other term, which occurs nowhere else, probably means either a crowd or an eager desire. Two plausible renderings are therefore left to choose between, that there is a crowd of their faces pressing forwards, or that their faces are set that way. Clarke reads the last clause simply, that they shall carry off innumerable captives.

The scoffing at kings is given a history. Gill names the invading king and the kings he carried captive, with the confederate on whom they had relied, and observes that the verse shows the vanity of trusting in princes for safety. Ellicott makes the point more exactly, that kings are deposed or enthroned at the invader's pleasure, and instances a tributary sovereign set on the throne, his successor deposed three years later, and a third made king in his place. Calvin adds what the taunt was aimed at: the Jews, excelling neither in numbers nor riches, were proud enough to look down on other nations and trusted vainly in a foreign confederacy, so the prophet tells them that kings would be mere sport to the Chaldeans.

The heaping of dust is explained as siegecraft. Clarke says they would need no formidable ramparts, since by sweeping the dust together they could make mounds enough to pass over the walls and take the city. Ellicott describes the practice more fully, that such mounds either raised the besieger to the level of the besieged so the engines could work, or formed an inclined plane up which men might march and take the place by escalade; and he notes the same method recorded of several ancient peoples, including a famous siege conducted by a Spartan king. Calvin states it in a phrase, that they will make a mound of the dust of the earth and so penetrate into every fortified city; and he closes the section by saying what the whole description was for, to cut off every hope from the Jews so that they might humble themselves, or else to take away every excuse if they did not repent, which, as he observes, is what happened.
11:
The changing mind is read three ways. Gill denies that the conqueror's purpose altered after the city fell, and takes it of a disposition changed for the worse by success: his mind was never good but always proud and cruel, and conquest made it worse. Clarke refers it to the later madness, when a beast's heart was given him and he was driven from the dwellings of men, brought on by his pride and by ascribing his success to his idols. Ellicott abandons the received rendering and gives, Then he sweeps by like a wind and passes; but he is guilty, making this his strength his god. The second half then turns abruptly from the human view of the conqueror to his appearance in God's sight: men see only an irresistible force crossing the earth like a whirlwind and are dazzled by the display, but the prophet pronounces his doom in the hour of triumph, and the description drops into a sudden anti-climax, that he is counted guilty. His guilt consists in exactly what men think glorious, his self-reliant pursuit of grandeur.

Calvin marks the turn as a change of audience: the prophet has addressed an irreclaimable people and now turns to the remnant, since there were always some faithful, however few, for whose sake God sent his prophets. Calvin makes it a rule: when the prophets denounce wrath they address the whole body, but when they add promises it is as though they called the faithful to a private conference and spoke in their ear. Gill describes the same movement, the prophet setting down comfort and then expostulating with God for good men stumbled that the wicked prosper while the righteous are afflicted.

Henry describes the position the prophet is caught in: looking about him he sees violence done by his own people, looking before him violence to be done against them, and it is hard to say which is the more melancholy sight. It is our duty, Henry says, to be affected with the iniquities and the calamities of the church alike, but we must take heed not to grow peevish and carry our resentments so far as to entertain hard thoughts of God; the world is bad and always was, and it is out of our power to mend it, but God governs it and will bring glory to himself out of all, so we must be better ourselves and long for the better world. The first truth the prophet lays hold of is that whatever comes God is still the Lord our God and our Holy One, and though the conquerors impute their power to their idols the God of Israel is the true and living one.

Calvin notices that the comfort is put as a question, which in Hebrew means the thing admits of no doubt, and that it is addressed to God and not to the wicked, since contending with them would be useless. Clarke sets the contrast his own way: idols change and their worshippers fail, but the Lord is eternal and those who trust him are safe. On the clause we shall not die, Clarke takes it that they shall not be totally exterminated, since the Chaldeans were raised up to correct but had no commission to destroy; he reports an emendation which by a transposition of letters yields God of truth instead, and says that elegant as it is, no manuscript and no ancient version supports it. Ellicott keeps the received words, glossing them that God's people may suffer but shall not be obliterated, and renders the rest literally, for judgment hast thou appointed him, and O Rock, for chastisement hast thou founded him, the title rendered mighty God being literally Rock. Wesley reduces the whole to glosses: the them are the Chaldean kingdom, the judgment is tempered with mercy, and the correction is to chastise and not destroy.
13:
Calvin distinguishes this complaint from the one that opened the chapter. There the prophet pleaded neither his own cause nor the people's but was roused by zeal for God's glory; here he comes down and expresses the feelings of men who had suffered injury under an enemy's tyranny, as those do who go to a judge and implore his protection. He also settles the grammar. Some render the first word as an imperative, but mistakenly, since the verse falls into two parts set against each other: the prophet reasons first from the nature of God, that being of pure eyes he cannot look on evil, and then states the opposite, that experience contradicts this, for the wicked exult. Keil and Delitzsch describes the same tension differently, that the confidence of the previous verse is not borne out by what God actually does, so the prophet lays the enigma before him and prays that his people be spared through the affliction; and he renders the opening as a question, art thou too pure of eye to behold evil? Ellicott puts it shortest: the prophet's confidence is tempered with anxious fear, and the triumph of a godless invader appears to impugn God's majesty.

Gill guards the first clause. God with his eyes of omniscience beholds all things good and evil, but does not look on the sins of men with pleasure or approbation, since they are contrary to his nature and breaches of his law; and though sin in general is included, Gill thinks a particular respect is had to the evil the Chaldeans did in invading the land, which, though permitted, could not be pleasing in his sight. Clarke answers the question rather than analysing it: all such questions are easily solved by a consideration of God's ineffable mercy, which leads him to suffer long and be kind, since he has no pleasure in the death of a sinner.

The comparison with fishes is worked out by every voice. Gill takes it that God suffers men to be used as fishes are, easily netted and common to whoever will take them, and hardly used among themselves besides; and he presses what makes this strange, that these were men made after God's image and a covenant people besides, of whom a more special providence might have been expected, and yet it looked as if no more care were taken of them than of fish. Wesley guards the verb, that God does not infuse cruel appetites but permits men to act according to the appetite already in them, so that the world, like the sea, is wholly oppression; the clause about no ruler he takes to mean there is none to defend the weak or restrain the mighty.

Clarke turns the figure into a portrait of the conqueror. We are easily taken, having no leader and no power to defend ourselves, while the invader is a fisherman constantly casting his nets and enclosing multitudes; always successful, he sacrifices to his own net, ascribing his conquests to his own power, without considering that he is himself only a net, thrown aside when done with or burnt. Calvin gives the complaint its full voice. The judgment is such as though God had turned away from men, neither checking the violence of the wicked nor setting his hand against them, so that each oppresses another as far as he exceeds him in power. Men were created after God's image, he has the prophet say, so why does no justice appear among them? When one devours another, and a single man oppresses almost the whole world, what can this mean? God seems to sport with human affairs; if he regards men as his children, why does he not defend them by his power? Yet we see one man so enraged and cruel as though the rest of the world were fish or reptiles.
15:
Gill notes that the prophet keeps the metaphor going and marks the different ways of taking fish: as fishermen take all they can with the angle, so the conqueror and his army take up all out of the sea of the world, ambitious to get every kingdom under their power, good and bad alike, since all were fish that came to their net. He suspects the angle stands for the alluring methods used first, the making of covenants and the drawing of a people into tribute. Wesley says the same more briefly, that they draw out all alike and destroy many together, and as if they could never have enough drive men into their nets.

The sacrifice to the net is explained literally by some and figuratively by others. Gill offers three senses, that they sacrificed to their idols and to fortune and the stars, or to their arms, or to their own valour and skill; and for the second he cites ancient reports of peoples who worshipped their spears, sacrificed to a scimitar, or held their swords for gods. Clarke states the charge bluntly, that this man had no God and cared for none but worshipped his armour and himself, and supports it from two Latin poets in whom a warrior invokes his own right hand as the only god he will acknowledge, one being struck down by thunder for the impiety. Relics survived in Europe, he adds, since military men swearing an oath lay a hand on the sword and formerly kissed it, and with most heroes the sword is both Bible and God. Ellicott allows that weapons may have been literally worshipped, instancing a people who sacrificed yearly to a sword as the emblem of their war god, but thinks the language probably metaphorical, and quotes a modern observation that a nation almost worshipped a newly invented gun as a goddess, idolising its own invention as though it could do what God alone can.

Calvin makes the sacrifice the climax of the complaint. It is abominable when the ungodly delight in their vices, but worse when they deride God himself, and these do not merely congratulate themselves while he spares them but rise up and blaspheme openly. The metaphor shows, he says, that the wicked are not only hardened by success but claim the praise of justice, counting whatever has succeeded to have been rightly done, and so dethroning God and putting themselves in his place. Wesley reduces it to a line, that they ascribe the praise of their victories to their own contrivance and power.

The closing question is read two ways. Gill and Clarke take it as asking whether the plundering shall simply go on, Gill picturing a fisherman who after a good draught empties the net in order to cast again, Clarke a man running from conquest to conquest; and Clarke adds that this sentence explains the allegory of the net. Ellicott renders it literally in the singular, shall he therefore empty his net, asking whether this voracious plunderer is to be allowed to consume his prey and cast the emptied net again and again. Calvin says all interpreters are mistaken here. They take the prophet to complain that the man casts again as soon as he has made a capture, whereas the question is whether he is ever to cast at all: how long will God permit such men to proceed to new plunders, like a hunter who grows more eager after taking a stag, or a fisherman who pursues his trade the harder once his boat is full? And Calvin marks what makes the forbearance so hard to bear, that the prophet speaks not of fish or of any single man but of many nations, and asks how long slaughters carried on through the whole world are to go unpunished, since of themselves they will never cease.
